screens.title: Designing for High Availability with AWS Services
screens.narratorSegment: High availability is about building systems that keep working when parts fail. In this chapter you will learn the practical AWS services and configurations that reduce downtime: Auto Scaling Groups combined with Elastic Load Balancers to keep compute capacity healthy across multiple Availability Zones, Multi‑AZ database and cache deployments for automatic failover, durable object storage with S3 including versioning and cross‑region replication, and Route 53 health checks with failover routing to steer traffic away from unhealthy endpoints. We’ll walk through concrete CLI examples and a short hands‑on activity that deploys a simple web app on an ALB and ASG across two AZs. Along the way you’ll see common mistakes to avoid, such as relying on instance‑level checks instead of application health, or keeping single external dependencies that defeat redundancy. By the end of the lesson you will understand not only which services to use but why synchronous replication, distributed placement, and verified health checks matter. Think of availability as a property achieved by deliberate redundancy and automated recovery — your goal is predictable failover and minimal manual intervention. As you explore, notice where a single misconfigured resource can turn a distributed system into a fragile one.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Designing for High Availability
Designing for High Availability with AWS Services
Build redundancy and automatic failover across compute, data, storage, and DNS.
In this lesson

You will learn how ASGs and ELBs work together, how Multi‑AZ deployments protect your databases and caches, how S3 durability and CRR provide durable storage, and how Route 53 health checks enable DNS failover.

Why it matters

Downtime costs users, revenue, and trust. Proper HA design reduces both unplanned outages and manual recovery time by using automation and distributed placement.

Explore Key Topics
ASG + ALB
Maintain desired capacity across AZs and route healthy traffic.
Multi‑AZ Databases
Synchronous standby replicas for automatic failover.
S3 & CRR
Durable object storage and cross‑region replication for DR.
Concept snapshot
Redundancy, synchronous replication, and verified health checks form a dependable high availability strategy.
Compute
ASG spans AZs. ALB routes to healthy targets and supports health checks that reflect application readiness.
Data
RDS Multi‑AZ and ElastiCache replication groups provide automatic failover with minimal manual steps.
Storage
S3 stores data across AZs with high durability; enable versioning and CRR for stronger protection and DR.
DNS
Route 53 health checks and failover routing ensure users reach healthy endpoints and support multi‑region strategies.
Coming up: a terminal‑style live demo of creating an ALB, a target group, and an ASG, plus RDS Multi‑AZ examples and a Route 53 failover pattern. Follow concept, then practice the hands‑on activity to internalize automatic failover behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these lessons you will implement and reason about high availability across layers. First, you will be able to configure Auto Scaling Groups and Elastic Load Balancers so your application runs with the desired capacity and client traffic is distributed across multiple Availability Zones. A concrete example is creating an ASG with a desired capacity of two instances and an ALB target group with a health‑check path, so unhealthy instances stop receiving traffic and are replaced automatically. Second, you will configure Multi‑AZ deployments for Amazon RDS and ElastiCache so a synchronous standby exists in another Availability Zone and failover happens automatically without manual intervention. You will practice verifying failover behavior and understanding the difference between read replicas and Multi‑AZ. These objectives emphasize operational reliability and the ability to validate system behavior under failure.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Deep Practice
screens.narratorSegment: Learning objectives are most useful when paired with clear validation and caution. You will practice deploying an ALB and ASG across at least two Availability Zones and then verify that traffic continues while individual instances are replaced. A hands‑on check is to terminate one EC2 instance and observe the ASG launch a replacement while the ALB continues to serve requests. For databases, you will enable Multi‑AZ and observe automatic failover behavior; practice verifying the new primary and check how read replicas differ in intent. For S3, you will enable versioning and set up cross‑region replication to protect against accidental overwrite and regional failures. Finally, for Route 53 health checks, you will create health checks that probe a real application path rather than a basic port check. Each objective includes a concrete verification step so you can confirm the system behaves as intended and avoid mistakes like blind reliance on instance status checks or a single external dependency.

keyIdea.title: Validation matters
keyIdea.text: Every HA feature should include a verification step and a check for hidden single points of failure.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Learning Objectives — Deep Practice
Objective validation checklist
  • Deploy ASG+ALB across two AZs and manually terminate one instance to confirm automatic replacement.
  • Enable RDS Multi‑AZ and observe failover to the standby during a simulated primary failure.
  • Turn on S3 versioning and perform an overwrite then recover the previous version.
  • Create Route 53 health checks that probe the application’s /health endpoint and test failover by disabling the target.
Common validation pitfalls
  • Checking only host status instead of application health can mask service failures.
  • Hardcoded IPs or single VPN connections can create hidden single points of failure.
  • Assuming read replicas provide automatic failover—read replicas are for scaling or DR, not primary HA.
Pro tip
Automate deployments using CloudFormation or CDK so your HA configuration is repeatable and auditable.
Check your understanding
After a failover, how would you verify RDS is writable and your application can resume normal traffic? Consider both DNS and connection pooling impacts.

screens.title: Auto Scaling Groups (ASG): purpose and behavior
screens.narratorSegment: An Auto Scaling Group keeps a specified number of instances running and replaces unhealthy ones automatically. Define a desired capacity, min, and max, and ASG will maintain that target by launching or terminating instances as needed. ASGs can span multiple Availability Zones so instances are distributed across physically separate data centers. The practical effect is that loss of a single instance or an entire AZ triggers replacement in healthy AZs, preserving capacity. A concrete example: create an ASG with desired capacity of two and public subnets in two AZs. If one AZ has an outage, the ASG will detect unhealthy instances and launch replacements in the remaining healthy AZ, returning the group to the desired capacity. A frequent misconception is to expect ASG to rebalance existing instances automatically across AZs; ASG focuses on maintaining count and health, not live rebalancing of running instances. Another pitfall is depending only on EC2 status checks for health — configure lifecycle hooks and application health checks so the group measures readiness, not just instance up/down status. Key takeaway: ASG supplies automated capacity resilience, but you must design health checks and placement thoughtfully to avoid hidden single points of failure.

keyIdea.title: ASG takeaway
keyIdea.text: ASGs automate instance replacement and can span AZs to maintain capacity, but health checks must reflect application readiness.

content.html:
Core Concept
Auto Scaling Groups
Maintain desired capacity and replace unhealthy instances automatically across AZs.
How it works
  • ASG monitors instance health and desired capacity; it launches or terminates instances to match the target.
  • Place an ASG in multiple public/private subnets across AZs to tolerate AZ failures.
  • Use EC2 and application health checks; consider lifecycle hooks for graceful shutdown and warm‑up.
Example scenario
ASG desired capacity 2 across AZ-a and AZ-b. Terminate one instance to confirm ASG launches a replacement and the ALB continues routing traffic to healthy instances.
Practical checklist
  • Define appropriate min/desired/max values to match load patterns and budget.
  • Configure health checks that probe application endpoints, not just OS up/down.
  • Use multiple AZs and attach the ASG to an ALB Target Group for routing resilience.
Common mistake
Relying only on instance status checks can leave an application unhealthy while ASG considers the instance healthy. Always include app-level health checks.

screens.title: Elastic Load Balancers: ALB and NLB roles
screens.narratorSegment: Elastic Load Balancers provide a single contact point for clients and distribute requests across registered targets in multiple Availability Zones. Application Load Balancers are ideal for HTTP and HTTPS traffic and support advanced request routing. Network Load Balancers are tuned for extreme performance, static IPs, and TCP/UDP traffic. Crucially for high availability, ELBs continuously monitor the health of their targets and remove unhealthy instances from rotation so users interact only with healthy application servers. A concrete example: register EC2 instances running Nginx in a target group with an ALB that checks the /health path every 30 seconds. If an instance fails its health checks, the ALB stops sending it traffic until it becomes healthy again. A common misconception is treating the ELB as a substitute for application readiness checks; instead, ensure health checks probe the application's ability to serve traffic. Also, ELBs do not replace ASG behavior — they complement ASGs by routing traffic while ASGs maintain capacity. Key takeaway: choose ALB or NLB based on protocol needs and ensure health checks reflect application readiness. Elastic Load Balancers: ALB and NLB roles means elbs route only to healthy targets and must be paired with meaningful application health checks to maintain user experience during failures.. In practical terms, distribute traffic and monitor target health for ha. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Elastic Load Balancers
Route client requests to healthy targets and integrate with ASG for capacity and resilience.
Compare ALB and NLB
Application Load Balancer
HTTP/HTTPS routing, host and path based rules, ideal for web apps.
Network Load Balancer
TCP/UDP, static IPs, ultra low latency and high throughput.
Health checks
  • Use an application endpoint such as /health that verifies database connectivity and request handling.
  • Set appropriate intervals and thresholds so transient spikes don’t mark targets unhealthy prematurely.
CLI example: create ALB and target group
aws elbv2 create-load-balancer \
    --name my-ha-alb \
    --subnets subnet-0abcdef1234567890 subnet-0fedcba9876543210 \
    --security-groups sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
    --scheme internet-facing \
    --type application

aws elbv2 create-target-group \
    --name my-app-targets \
    --protocol HTTP \
    --port 80 \
    --vpc-id vpc-0abcdef1234567890 \
    --health-check-protocol HTTP \
    --health-check-path /health \
    --health-check-interval-seconds 30 \
    --health-check-timeout-seconds 5 \
    --healthy-threshold-count 2 \
    --unhealthy-threshold-count 2
Example note
This sequence sets up a basic ALB and target group with a health check path. Automate it with CloudFormation or CDK for repeatable HA deployments.

screens.title: Setting up an ALB, Target Group, and Listener
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying an ALB with a healthy target group and a listener is a common start for a highly available web tier. The process has three clear steps: create the ALB, create the target group with meaningful health checks, and create a listener that forwards traffic. Start by selecting public subnets in different AZs and a security group allowing the required ports. Next, create the target group with an HTTP health check that probes a path such as /health; this ensures the load balancer verifies application readiness rather than just host availability. Finally, create a listener for port 80 or 443 that forwards to your target group. Automating these steps with scripts or templates reduces errors and guarantees the ALB and target group are consistently configured across environments. A common misconception is assuming default health checks are sufficient — tune the path, interval, and thresholds to your application. After creating these components, register instances or attach the ASG so the ALB receives targets dynamically and health checks control traffic routing. Practice these steps in a sandbox before applying them to production.

keyIdea.title: Process takeaway
keyIdea.text: Create ALB, define a target group with app-level health checks, and create a listener that forwards traffic to healthy targets.

content.html:
Process Flow
ALB → Target Group → Listener
Steps
1. Create ALB
Choose public subnets in at least two AZs and an appropriate security group.
2. Create Target Group
Set protocol and port, and a health check path such as /health that validates application readiness.
3. Create Listener
Create a listener on port 80 or 443 that forwards to the target group and verify routing behavior.
Tip
Attach an ASG to the target group so instances register automatically and are balanced across AZs.
CLI snippet
# create load balancer
aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --name my-ha-alb --subnets subnet-0a subnet-0b --security-groups sg-aaa --scheme internet-facing --type application

# create target group
aws elbv2 create-target-group --name my-app-targets --protocol HTTP --port 80 --vpc-id vpc-0 --health-check-protocol HTTP --health-check-path /health
Validation
After launch, wait for targets to become healthy, then browse the ALB DNS and refresh to verify requests hit different instances.

screens.title: ASG + ALB in practice: behavior during failure
screens.narratorSegment: When an instance fails, the ALB and ASG each play a distinct role to preserve availability. The ALB detects failing targets through its health check and stops sending traffic to those instances. Simultaneously, the ASG inspects instance health, and if an instance is unhealthy or terminated, it launches a replacement to return to the desired capacity. A practical walkthrough: imagine an ASG with desired capacity 3 across three AZs and an ALB fronting them. If one instance becomes unhealthy, the ALB removes it from rotation immediately, so user requests go to the remaining healthy instances. The ASG then replaces the unhealthy instance, potentially in a different AZ if the original AZ is impaired. A common misconception is expecting zero impact; while routing continues, user capacity may temporarily be reduced until the ASG launches replacements. Also watch for connection draining and session persistence considerations — enable connection draining or deregistration delays so in-flight requests complete before an instance is removed. Finally, automated replacement and routing ensure the system recovers without manual intervention, but verification and monitoring are essential so you can measure recovery timelines and user impact.

keyIdea.text: ALB removes unhealthy targets immediately while ASG replaces instances to restore capacity; temporary capacity reduction is normal during recovery.

content.html:
Architecture
ASG + ALB recovery flow
Recovery sequence
  1. ALB health checks fail for the instance; the ALB stops routing to it.
  2. The ASG marks the instance unhealthy and terminates it (or replaces it), then launches a new instance.
  3. The new instance registers with the target group; after passing health checks, it receives traffic.
Practical notes
Expect a temporary capacity dip; tune deregistration delay and lifecycle hooks to allow graceful shutdowns, and monitor the ASG launch times to ensure capacity returns within your SLA.
Scenario example
ASG desired capacity 3. One AZ reports degraded network; two instances in that AZ fail health checks. The ALB stops routing to them, the ASG launches replacements in healthy AZs, and capacity returns to three. Measure how long the ALB takes to remove targets and how long the ASG takes to launch replacements to understand RTO impact.
Check your understanding
Why is it important to tune health check thresholds and deregistration delays? Consider false positives and in‑flight requests.
Key takeaway

ALB and ASG together maintain availability: ALB keeps traffic on healthy targets while ASG restores capacity automatically; both need correct tuning for smooth recovery.

screens.title: RDS Multi‑AZ deployments
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon RDS Multi‑AZ creates a synchronous standby replica of your primary database in a different Availability Zone. Writes are synchronously replicated so the standby has up‑to‑date data and can take over automatically in case of primary failure, AZ outage, or scheduled maintenance. This reduces both downtime and data loss compared to manual recovery. A concrete example is enabling Multi‑AZ for a PostgreSQL instance: AWS provisions a standby and handles failover for you; the failover typically completes within a couple of minutes. Be careful to distinguish Multi‑AZ from read replicas: read replicas provide read scaling and can be promoted for DR, but they are not a substitute for Multi‑AZ automatic failover within a region. A common pitfall is assuming zero downtime; while failover is automatic, it usually takes between 60 and 120 seconds, and client reconnection behavior may affect application availability. Key steps include testing failover in a non‑production environment, validating that clients retry connections appropriately, and monitoring RTO and RPO to ensure they meet your SLAs. RDS Multi‑AZ deployments means multi‑az provides automatic failover via a synchronous standby in another az, minimizing downtime and data loss compared to manual recovery strategies.. In practical terms, synchronous standby replicas for automatic failover. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
RDS Multi‑AZ
Synchronous standby replicas that enable automatic failover within a Region.
How it's provisioned
  • A primary instance and a synchronous standby in a separate AZ.
  • Writes are synchronously replicated to the standby; upon failure, RDS promotes the standby to primary.
  • Failover is automatic but not instant — test reconnection behavior of your client drivers.
Contrast with read replicas
Read replicas replicate asynchronously and are primarily for read scaling or cross‑region DR. They are not guaranteed to be up to date for automatic failover and require manual promotion unless part of a managed failover plan.
Validation step
In a test environment, force a failover and measure the time for the standby to become primary and how your application reconnects. Tune client retry logic accordingly.
Key takeaway

Multi‑AZ is the recommended configuration for RDS when automatic failover and minimized data loss are required within a Region.

screens.title: ElastiCache Multi‑AZ and replication groups
screens.narratorSegment: ElastiCache can be configured for high availability using replication groups and Multi‑AZ placement. For Redis, use a replication group with a primary and replicas in separate AZs; ElastiCache can promote a replica if the primary fails. This keeps the caching layer available and reduces the impact of AZ outages on application performance. For Memcached, distribute nodes across AZs and rely on client‑side sharding and node replacement to maintain capacity. A concrete example: create a Redis replication group with automatic failover enabled so when the primary fails, a synchronous-like replica takes over with minimal disruption. A common misconception is assuming caches are stateless and need no HA; while caches can be recreated, losing warmed caches can severely impact application latency and database load. Therefore, configure replication and Multi‑AZ placement when cache availability is important. Validate by simulating node failure and observing promotion and client reconnection behavior. Key takeaway: treat cache availability with the same seriousness as databases when performance and stability are at stake. ElastiCache Multi‑AZ and replication groups means configure replication groups and multi‑az placement for redis; distribute memcached nodes and validate failover to preserve cache availability and performance.. In practical terms, keep your in-memory cache available during failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition
ElastiCache Multi‑AZ
Replication groups and AZ distribution preserve cache availability and reduce database pressure during failures.
Redis replication groups
  • Create a replication group with automatic failover enabled to promote a replica if the primary fails.
  • Place nodes in different AZs to tolerate AZ outages.
  • Test failover and client reconnection to confirm minimal impact.

Memcached relies on client-side sharding and node replacement; distribute nodes across AZs so losing one node does not eliminate the entire cache. Warm caches as part of bootstrapping where possible.
Common mistake
Assuming a cache miss is harmless. Losing warm cache state can spike database load and increase latency.
Key takeaway

Treat cache HA as a first‑class concern: replication, AZ placement, and failover testing keep application latency predictable during failures.

screens.narratorSegment: Amazon S3 is designed for very high durability by storing objects redundantly across multiple devices and Availability Zones. For operational protection enable versioning to recover from accidental deletes or overwrites, and configure cross‑region replication (CRR) to copy objects to a bucket in another Region for disaster recovery. For example, enabling versioning protects prior object states so you can restore previous versions after accidental changes. CRR automatically copies new objects or new versions to the target bucket in the destination Region. Key takeaway: combine S3 durability with versioning and CRR for robust object protection and recovery strategies. screens.narratorSegment: Route 53 health checks and failover routing let DNS direct clients to healthy endpoints. Create health checks that probe application endpoints such as an ALB DNS name or a dedicated /health URL. Hands-on Activity
Launch Template user data
Use this script in your Launch Template user data to install Nginx and display AZ information.
#!/bin/bash
yum update -y
yum install -y nginx
systemctl start nginx
systemctl enable nginx
AZ=$(curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/placement/availability-zone)
HOST=$(hostname -f)
echo "<h1>Hello from ${HOST} in AZ ${AZ}</h1>" > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
Activity steps
  1. Create a VPC with at least two public subnets in separate AZs and appropriate route tables.
  2. Create a Launch Template that uses the user data above and an AMI with Amazon Linux 2.
  3. Create a target group for port 80 and an ALB across the public subnets; set health check path to /.
  4. Create an ASG with desired capacity 2, min 2, max 4, using the Launch Template and attach it to the target group.
  5. Validate by visiting the ALB DNS and refreshing to see different AZ hostnames; terminate an instance and observe replacement.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Even well‑designed HA systems can fail if a single non‑redundant dependency exists. Common pitfalls include hardcoded IP addresses, a single on‑premises VPN or NAT gateway that is not redundant, application configuration that points to a single endpoint, and health checks that only confirm host reachability rather than application readiness. Best practices are straightforward: remove hardcoded endpoints, distribute components across AZs, use managed services where possible, and design health checks that exercise critical paths such as database connectivity and request handling. Another important best practice is to automate HA setup using CloudFormation or CDK so your configuration is repeatable and auditable. A practical verification step is to perform controlled failures in a staging environment: terminate instances, disable an AZ subnet, and observe ALB and ASG behavior as well as RDS failover. A misconception to guard against is assuming that adding more instances without correct health checks guarantees availability. Instrument your system with monitoring and alerts so you detect and respond to unexpected behaviors. The core lesson is that HA requires both infrastructure redundancy and correct operational practices. Common pitfalls and best practices means design ha holistically: remove single points of failure, use meaningful health checks, and automate deployments to ensure repeatable resilience.. Pitfalls vs Best Practices

  • Hardcoded IPs or single VPN links.
  • Health checks that verify only host up/down.
  • Assuming read replicas equal automatic failover.
Best Practice
  • Design for redundancy across AZs and services.

Simulate failures in staging and observe ALB deregistration, ASG replacement, and RDS failover so you can quantify RTO and RPO.

If you have a single VPN to on‑prem systems and it fails, your application may be unreachable even if all AWS components are healthy. Remove single external dependencies or introduce redundant network paths to avoid this class of failure.
Key takeaway

High availability succeeds when architecture, health checks, automation, and verification work together. Address hidden single points of failure and practice failovers regularly.

fullNarratorScript:
High availability is about building systems that keep working when parts fail. In this chapter you will learn the practical AWS services and configurations that reduce downtime: Auto Scaling Groups combined with Elastic Load Balancers to keep compute capacity healthy across multiple Availability Zones, Multi‑AZ database and cache deployments for automatic failover, durable object storage with S3 including versioning and cross‑region replication, and Route 53 health checks with failover routing to steer traffic away from unhealthy endpoints. We’ll walk through concrete CLI examples and a short hands‑on activity that deploys a simple web app on an ALB and ASG across two AZs. Along the way you’ll see common mistakes to avoid, such as relying on instance‑level checks instead of application health, or keeping single external dependencies that defeat redundancy. By the end of the lesson you will understand not only which services to use but why synchronous replication, distributed placement, and verified health checks matter. Think of availability as a property achieved by deliberate redundancy and automated recovery — your goal is predictable failover and minimal manual intervention. As you explore, notice where a single misconfigured resource can turn a distributed system into a fragile one.

By the end of these lessons you will implement and reason about high availability across layers. First, you will be able to configure Auto Scaling Groups and Elastic Load Balancers so your application runs with the desired capacity and client traffic is distributed across multiple Availability Zones. A concrete example is creating an ASG with a desired capacity of two instances and an ALB target group with a health‑check path, so unhealthy instances stop receiving traffic and are replaced automatically. Second, you will configure Multi‑AZ deployments for Amazon RDS and ElastiCache so a synchronous standby exists in another Availability Zone and failover happens automatically without manual intervention. You will practice verifying failover behavior and understanding the difference between read replicas and Multi‑AZ. These objectives emphasize operational reliability and the ability to validate system behavior under failure.

Learning objectives are most useful when paired with clear validation and caution. You will practice deploying an ALB and ASG across at least two Availability Zones and then verify that traffic continues while individual instances are replaced. A hands‑on check is to terminate one EC2 instance and observe the ASG launch a replacement while the ALB continues to serve requests. For databases, you will enable Multi‑AZ and observe automatic failover behavior; practice verifying the new primary and check how read replicas differ in intent. For S3, you will enable versioning and set up cross‑region replication to protect against accidental overwrite and regional failures. Finally, for Route 53 health checks, you will create health checks that probe a real application path rather than a basic port check. Each objective includes a concrete verification step so you can confirm the system behaves as intended and avoid mistakes like blind reliance on instance status checks or a single external dependency.

An Auto Scaling Group keeps a specified number of instances running and replaces unhealthy ones automatically. Define a desired capacity, min, and max, and ASG will maintain that target by launching or terminating instances as needed. ASGs can span multiple Availability Zones so instances are distributed across physically separate data centers. The practical effect is that loss of a single instance or an entire AZ triggers replacement in healthy AZs, preserving capacity. A concrete example: create an ASG with desired capacity of two and public subnets in two AZs. If one AZ has an outage, the ASG will detect unhealthy instances and launch replacements in the remaining healthy AZ, returning the group to the desired capacity. A frequent misconception is to expect ASG to rebalance existing instances automatically across AZs; ASG focuses on maintaining count and health, not live rebalancing of running instances. Another pitfall is depending only on EC2 status checks for health — configure lifecycle hooks and application health checks so the group measures readiness, not just instance up/down status. Key takeaway: ASG supplies automated capacity resilience, but you must design health checks and placement thoughtfully to avoid hidden single points of failure.

Elastic Load Balancers provide a single contact point for clients and distribute requests across registered targets in multiple Availability Zones. Application Load Balancers are ideal for HTTP and HTTPS traffic and support advanced request routing. Network Load Balancers are tuned for extreme performance, static IPs, and TCP/UDP traffic. Crucially for high availability, ELBs continuously monitor the health of their targets and remove unhealthy instances from rotation so users interact only with healthy application servers. A concrete example: register EC2 instances running Nginx in a target group with an ALB that checks the /health path every 30 seconds. If an instance fails its health checks, the ALB stops sending it traffic until it becomes healthy again. A common misconception is treating the ELB as a substitute for application readiness checks; instead, ensure health checks probe the application's ability to serve traffic. Also, ELBs do not replace ASG behavior — they complement ASGs by routing traffic while ASGs maintain capacity. Key takeaway: choose ALB or NLB based on protocol needs and ensure health checks reflect application readiness. Elastic Load Balancers: ALB and NLB roles means elbs route only to healthy targets and must be paired with meaningful application health checks to maintain user experience during failures.. In practical terms, distribute traffic and monitor target health for ha. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Deploying an ALB with a healthy target group and a listener is a common start for a highly available web tier. The process has three clear steps: create the ALB, create the target group with meaningful health checks, and create a listener that forwards traffic. Start by selecting public subnets in different AZs and a security group allowing the required ports. Next, create the target group with an HTTP health check that probes a path such as /health; this ensures the load balancer verifies application readiness rather than just host availability. Finally, create a listener for port 80 or 443 that forwards to your target group. Automating these steps with scripts or templates reduces errors and guarantees the ALB and target group are consistently configured across environments. A common misconception is assuming default health checks are sufficient — tune the path, interval, and thresholds to your application. After creating these components, register instances or attach the ASG so the ALB receives targets dynamically and health checks control traffic routing. Practice these steps in a sandbox before applying them to production.

When an instance fails, the ALB and ASG each play a distinct role to preserve availability. The ALB detects failing targets through its health check and stops sending traffic to those instances. Simultaneously, the ASG inspects instance health, and if an instance is unhealthy or terminated, it launches a replacement to return to the desired capacity. A practical walkthrough: imagine an ASG with desired capacity 3 across three AZs and an ALB fronting them. If one instance becomes unhealthy, the ALB removes it from rotation immediately, so user requests go to the remaining healthy instances. The ASG then replaces the unhealthy instance, potentially in a different AZ if the original AZ is impaired. A common misconception is expecting zero impact; while routing continues, user capacity may temporarily be reduced until the ASG launches replacements. Also watch for connection draining and session persistence considerations — enable connection draining or deregistration delays so in-flight requests complete before an instance is removed. Finally, automated replacement and routing ensure the system recovers without manual intervention, but verification and monitoring are essential so you can measure recovery timelines and user impact.

Amazon RDS Multi‑AZ creates a synchronous standby replica of your primary database in a different Availability Zone. Writes are synchronously replicated so the standby has up‑to‑date data and can take over automatically in case of primary failure, AZ outage, or scheduled maintenance. This reduces both downtime and data loss compared to manual recovery. A concrete example is enabling Multi‑AZ for a PostgreSQL instance: AWS provisions a standby and handles failover for you; the failover typically completes within a couple of minutes. Be careful to distinguish Multi‑AZ from read replicas: read replicas provide read scaling and can be promoted for DR, but they are not a substitute for Multi‑AZ automatic failover within a region. A common pitfall is assuming zero downtime; while failover is automatic, it usually takes between 60 and 120 seconds, and client reconnection behavior may affect application availability. Key steps include testing failover in a non‑production environment, validating that clients retry connections appropriately, and monitoring RTO and RPO to ensure they meet your SLAs. RDS Multi‑AZ deployments means multi‑az provides automatic failover via a synchronous standby in another az, minimizing downtime and data loss compared to manual recovery strategies.. In practical terms, synchronous standby replicas for automatic failover. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ElastiCache can be configured for high availability using replication groups and Multi‑AZ placement. For Redis, use a replication group with a primary and replicas in separate AZs; ElastiCache can promote a replica if the primary fails. This keeps the caching layer available and reduces the impact of AZ outages on application performance. For Memcached, distribute nodes across AZs and rely on client‑side sharding and node replacement to maintain capacity. A concrete example: create a Redis replication group with automatic failover enabled so when the primary fails, a synchronous-like replica takes over with minimal disruption. A common misconception is assuming caches are stateless and need no HA; while caches can be recreated, losing warmed caches can severely impact application latency and database load. Therefore, configure replication and Multi‑AZ placement when cache availability is important. Validate by simulating node failure and observing promotion and client reconnection behavior.
